title: Separations and Purifications
description: Choose and interpret solubility, volatility, and chromatographic separations.
objectives: Calculate Rf and match chromatography methods

lessons.label: Extraction, filtration, and recrystallization
lessons.title: Extraction, filtration, and recrystallization
lessons.tag: Change solubility to move a compound

cards.rule: Liquid–liquid extraction partitions solutes between immiscible phases. Acid/base chemistry can turn a neutral acid or base into a more water-soluble ion. Recrystallization exploits high hot-solvent and low cold-solvent solubility of the desired compound. Hot gravity filtration removes insoluble material; vacuum filtration collects crystals.
cards.cue: For an acid: deprotonate to move toward water, then acidify to recover the neutral form.
cards.trap: The organic layer is not always on top; density determines position. Keep track of which layer contains the target. Several smaller extractions can outperform one using the same total solvent volume. A wash removes impurities while retaining the target in its phase.
cards.app: Acid/base extraction separates acidic, basic, and neutral drug-like compounds by controlling their charge and partitioning.

steps.label: 1. Neutral aromatic acid
steps.text: Benzoic acid combines a nonpolar aromatic region with a polar acid group. Its partitioning depends on both molecular structure and ionization.

steps.label: 2. Ionize the acid
steps.text: At sufficiently high pH, benzoate predominates and is generally more water soluble than neutral benzoic acid. Acidifying can regenerate neutral acid for recovery when solubility conditions permit.

steps.label: 3. Recrystallize the recovered solid
steps.text: Use a suitable solvent system in which the desired solid dissolves hot and crystallizes on cooling. Soluble impurities should remain mainly in the mother liquor; insoluble impurities can be filtered before cooling.

lessons.label: Distillation and volatility
lessons.title: Distillation and volatility
lessons.tag: Vapor is enriched in the more volatile component

cards.rule: Distillation separates liquids by volatility. Simple distillation suits sufficiently different volatilities; fractional distillation adds repeated vaporization/condensation for closer boiling mixtures. Lower pressure lowers boiling temperature, so vacuum distillation can help with high-boiling or heat-sensitive liquids.
cards.cue: Fractionating column = repeated equilibrium stages. Vacuum = lower boiling temperature.
cards.trap: Boiling-point cutoffs are heuristics, not universal rules. Azeotropes can limit ordinary distillation. Distillation does not guarantee a pure first fraction merely because one component has a lower boiling point.
cards.app: Choose a method based on volatility, thermal stability, pressure, and mixture behavior; record boiling temperatures with pressure.

steps.label: 1. A molecular property
steps.text: Toluene is a neutral volatile organic liquid. Intermolecular interactions influence its vapor pressure and boiling behavior; the structure alone does not supply an exact boiling point.

steps.label: 2. Choose a method
steps.text: For a hypothetical close-boiling mixture, fractionation can improve enrichment. If the material decomposes near its atmospheric boiling point, reducing pressure may allow a lower operating temperature.

lessons.label: TLC and normal-phase columns
lessons.title: TLC and normal-phase columns
lessons.tag: Retention competes with the mobile phase

cards.rule: In normal-phase TLC, polar silica is stationary and solvent moves upward by capillary action. Stronger attraction to silica generally lowers Rf. Rf = distance traveled by spot center / distance traveled by solvent front, both measured from the baseline. A stronger eluent usually raises Rf on silica.
cards.cue: Stronger stationary-phase binding → slower travel. Rf has no units.
cards.trap: Rf depends on plate, solvent, and conditions; it is not a permanent molecular constant. Equal Rf is supporting evidence, not definitive identification. In reversed-phase systems the stationary phase is nonpolar, so polarity trends differ.
cards.app: TLC can follow reaction progress by comparing starting-material and product spots under the same conditions; a single spot is not proof of absolute purity.

steps.label: 1. Identify polar interactions
steps.text: The carboxyl group can interact strongly with silica. Actual retention depends on the eluent, ionization, and other experimental details.

diagram.caption: Normal-phase TLC trend model: increasing relative eluent strength moves both model spots upward.

steps.label: 2. Calculate normalized travel
steps.text: A spot traveling 1.8 cm while the front travels 6.0 cm has Rf=0.30. Use the same origin for both measurements. The schematic slider is a trend illustration, not a prediction for this molecule.

diagram.caption: Schematic plate; baseline and solvent front define the distance ratio.

lessons.label: Choose a chromatography method
lessons.title: Choose a chromatography method
lessons.tag: Match the separation to a molecular property

cards.rule: Ion exchange separates by charge: a positively charged anion exchanger binds anions; a negatively charged cation exchanger binds cations. Size exclusion separates by access to pores, with larger species generally eluting first. Affinity chromatography uses specific binding. GC requires adequate volatility and thermal stability; HPLC uses a liquid mobile phase under pressure and can handle many nonvolatile analytes.
cards.cue: Ion exchange: charge. Size exclusion: pore access. Affinity: specific interaction.
cards.trap: Small molecules enter more pore volume and usually elute later in size exclusion. “Anion exchanger” names the species it binds, not the resin’s own charge. Reversed-phase HPLC usually retains hydrophobic analytes more strongly than polar ones under comparable conditions.
cards.app: Protein purification often combines orthogonal methods: charge, size, and affinity. Choose based on protein stability as well as separation power.

steps.label: 1. Charge depends on conditions
steps.text: This peptide has ionizable termini. At pH above its pI it tends toward negative net charge, which can favor binding to a positive anion-exchange resin. Real proteins may have many additional ionizable side chains.

steps.label: 2. Choose by analyte behavior
steps.text: An ionic nonvolatile peptide is usually better suited to a liquid-phase method than direct GC without derivatization. Larger proteins can be separated by hydrodynamic size using porous beads; mass alone is not the only determinant.

exercises.label: Plan an acid–base separation
exercises.title: Plan an acid–base separation

stages.explanation: G, H, and I form COOH.
hints: Find the carbon outside the ring bonded to two O atoms.
Include the carbon and both oxygens.

stages.prompt: To favor transfer of this acid into an aqueous phase, choose…
options: A pH well above its pKa
A pH far below its pKa in every case
stages.explanation: Deprotonation generates a more water-soluble carboxylate.
hints: Use ionization to change partitioning.
High pH removes the acidic proton.

stages.prompt: To collect recrystallized solid from cold mother liquor, use…
options: Hot gravity filtration to keep all product dissolved
stages.explanation: Vacuum filtration collects crystals and removes liquid efficiently.
hints: Identify whether the target is solid or dissolved.
The crystals are the desired residue.

exercises.summary: Ionization moves the acid; crystallization and filtration can recover it.

exercises.label: Choose the separation conditions
exercises.title: Choose the separation conditions

stages.prompt: A close-boiling liquid mixture is generally better separated with…
stages.explanation: A fractionating column provides repeated vapor–liquid equilibration.
hints: Both components are liquids.
Repeated enrichment helps when volatility differences are small.

stages.prompt: Reducing external pressure generally makes the boiling temperature…
stages.explanation: Boiling occurs when vapor pressure equals external pressure; that equality is reached at a lower temperature.
hints: Use the condition for boiling.
Less external pressure requires less vapor pressure.

stages.prompt: Which can limit ordinary fractional distillation?
options: The presence of any carbon atom
stages.explanation: An azeotropic composition can distill without composition change under the given conditions.
hints: Consider nonideal mixture behavior.
A column cannot always surpass the equilibrium limit.

exercises.summary: Use fractionation for close volatilities and vacuum when lower temperature is useful.

exercises.label: Calculate and interpret Rf
exercises.title: Calculate and interpret Rf

stages.prompt: A spot center travels 1.8 cm and the solvent front 6.0 cm. What is Rf?
hints: Divide spot distance by front distance.
Both distances start at the baseline.

stages.prompt: On normal-phase silica, a stronger eluent usually makes Rf…
stages.explanation: A stronger eluent competes more effectively with analyte–silica interactions.
hints: Consider the balance between mobile and stationary phase attraction.
More elution usually moves the spot farther.

stages.prompt: Two compounds with the same Rf on one plate are…
stages.explanation: Co-migration under one condition is not unique structural identification.
hints: Different molecules can have similar retention.
Use another condition or independent analytical evidence.

exercises.summary: Rf is a condition-dependent distance ratio.

diagram.caption: Explore the normal-phase trend; use the distances in the question for the calculation.

exercises.label: Match a protein to a column
exercises.title: Match a protein to a column

stages.prompt: A protein at pH 7 with pI 5 tends to have what net charge?
stages.explanation: At pH above pI, net charge is generally negative.
hints: Compare pH with pI.
Raising pH removes protons.

stages.prompt: Which resin would electrostatically bind that protein?
stages.explanation: A positive resin attracts the negatively charged protein.
hints: Opposite charges attract.
Name the exchanger by the ions it binds.

stages.prompt: In ideal size exclusion, larger molecules within the useful separation range usually elute…
stages.explanation: Larger molecules access less pore volume and take a shorter effective path.
hints: Smaller molecules explore more pores.
Pore entry delays elution.

exercises.summary: Charge and pore access give distinct separation strategies.
